en: The Secret Essential Methods for Treating the Illnesses of Dhyāna, Volume One.
Translated by the Song Dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng.
The Seventy-Two Methods for Treating the Illnesses of Mental Disturbance in Āraṇya Practice. By the Venerable Śāriputra.
Regarding the question, it is excerpted from the *Saṃyukta Āgama* in the section on forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

On the fifteenth day of the fifth month of summer, five hundred Śākya bhikṣus were practicing the dharma of araṇya in the Bamboo Grove, cultivating the twelvefold mental training; through ānāpāna, they entered the Vaiḍūrya samādhi.

At that time, King Prasenajit had a crown prince named Virūḍhaka. Accompanied by five hundred sons of elders, he was riding a great fragrant elephant near the Jeta Grove, performing the Nārāyaṇa dance; he then intoxicated the elephants and engaged in elephant-fighting games.
There was a black elephant amidst a row of lotuses, its sound loathsome and resembling a thunderclap, while its intermediate, faint cries were like the howling of kittens.

The Śākya bhikṣus—Candanā and Upacandanā, among others—were struck with terror and their hair stood on end; they gave rise to mad and deluded thoughts regarding the element of wind (vāyudhātu), and rising from their meditative concentration, they were like intoxicated elephants galloping away, impossible to restrain.
The Venerable Ānanda commanded the bhikṣus:
"Shut the doors of the cells firmly; these sons of the Śākyas have now gone mad and might cause injury or destruction.
The community of bhikṣus then went to where Śāriputra was and said to him:
“Venerable One!
Your wisdom, as you know it, is unobstructed, like the supreme victory banner of Śakra, Lord of Devas, reaching everywhere without fear.
We pray that out of compassion you will rescue these sons of the Śākyas from the suffering of their madness.”

At that time, Śāriputra rose from his seat, took Ānanda by the hand, and went to where the Buddha was. He circumambulated the Buddha three times, paid homage to him, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for all beings, will explain how to treat these five kinds of ailments that cause future forest-dwelling bhikṣus to lose their sanity: first, due to chaotic sounds; second, due to ill repute; third, due to gain and offerings; fourth, due to external winds; and fifth, due to internal winds. How should these five types of illnesses be cured?
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me.

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled, and five-colored rays of light issued from his mouth, circled him seven times, and returned to enter through the crown of his head. He then addressed Śāriputra:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.”

"If there is a practitioner who practices in the forest (āraṇya) and cultivates the twelve modes of mental cultivation, yet due to external harsh sounds contacting the internal faculties during ānāpāna meditation, the four hundred and four channels cause the mind to become suddenly agitated because it is held too tightly."
Because the wind-force is powerful, one first becomes insane; as the heart-vessels pulsate and the five winds enter the throat, one first utters evil speech.

One should instruct this practitioner to consume ghee, honey, and harītakī, and to bind the mind to a single point. First, they should visualize a crystal-colored mirror and observe their own body within that mirror performing various acts of madness.
Having seen this, one should further contemplate it and say:
"In a clear mirror you see your own body performing acts of madness and folly; your parents and kinsmen all see you performing inauspicious deeds."
"I shall now teach you the method for abandoning madness and delusion; you should remember and understand it. First, I shall teach the removal of sound.

Regarding the method for removing sound: "Lift the tongue toward the palate and visualize two maṇi jewels within the roots of the two ears. At the tips of these wish-fulfilling jewels, there are drops like droplets of milk; from within each drop flows clarified butter (ghṛta), which moistens the auditory roots so that they no longer receive sound."
Even if a great sound occurs, one remains utterly unmoved, like oil that has saturated [a surface].

Once this visualization is accomplished, next visualize a single ninefold vajra canopy emerging from the King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels to cover the practitioner’s body; beneath it are vajra flowers, upon which the practitioner sits.

There is a mountain of vajra, which encircles the practitioner on all four sides; its interior is dense and secluded, utterly devoid of external sound. Within each of these mountains, seven Buddhas are seated, expounding the four foundations of mindfulness for the practitioner.
At that time, being silent and hearing no external sounds, one follows the Buddha’s teaching; this is called the Dharma-gate for Eliminating Distraction, which removes the perception of evil sounds.
He addressed Śāriputra:
“You practitioners should cultivate this diligently and take care not to forget it; this is called the Dharma for treating a distracted and inverted mind.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra! Having already eliminated external sounds, one should eliminate internal sounds.
'Internal sounds' refers to the movement of the six sense faculties caused by external sounds, which results in the inversion of the mental continuum."
The five kinds of evil winds enter through the heart-vessel; because the wind agitates the mind, one may sing, dance, or undergo various transformations.
You should instruct them in the practice of washing the mind through contemplation.

"As for the practitioner who purifies the mind through contemplation, they first observe their own mind, causing it to gradually become as clear as a fire-jewel—wherein the four hundred and four channels are like *vaiḍūrya* crystal, and golden plantain stalks extend right to the heart’s edge. The fire-jewel emits a breath that is neither cold nor hot, neither coarse nor subtle, which is used to permeate all the channels."
Visualize a Brahmā King holding a maṇi mirror that illuminates the practitioner’s chest.
At that time, the practitioner observes his own chest as being like the king of wish-fulfilling jewels (cintāmaṇi-rāja), bright, pure, and lovely, with a fire-gem as its heart.

In the palm of the Great Brahmā King is a wheel-turning seal (*cakravarti-mudrā*); within the wheel-turning seal is a white lotus; upon the white lotus is a celestial youth holding milk in his hand, which issues forth from the king of wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi-rāja*) to irrigate all the channels.

The milk gradually descends to the tip of the heart. The youth holds two needles—one golden-yellow and the other blue—and places two golden flowers on both sides of the heart, piercing them with the needles. After seven piercings, the heart returns to its natural softness.

"As before, he again washes his heart with milk; the drops of milk flow and enter the large intestine. Once the large intestine is full, they enter the small intestine. When the small intestine is full, the milk flows out in an unceasing stream, entering the mouths of the eighty thousand families of worms. These worms become satiated throughout the interior of the body, and the milk flows into all three hundred and thirty-six joints of the bones, pervading them entirely."

Thereafter, one visualizes a single pool of milk, in which a white lotus flower grows; the practitioner sits upon it and bathes in the milk. One visualizes cotton-wool (*tūla*) like white lotuses encircling the body seven times, with the practitioner situated in their midst.

The Brahma King personally took his own breast milk and had the practitioner rinse their mouth with it; once the practitioner had rinsed, the Brahma King held a canopy over them. Within that Brahma King’s canopy, they universally beheld all supreme realms and regained their original mind, free from any confusion.

When the Buddha spoke these words, the five hundred Śākya bhikṣus followed his instructions one by one. Their minds immediately became cool and serene; they contemplated form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. No longer craving the world, they attained a thorough understanding of the dharma of emptiness, and suddenly they recovered their original minds.

Having shattered eight billion blazing fetters, he attained the stage of *srotāpanna*; gradually practicing and training, he attained the state of an *arhat*, endowed with the three knowledges (*trividyā*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).

At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly; this is called the method for treating the internal winds of the four great elements with gentleness.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

If a practitioner wishes to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they should skillfully observe the states of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their increase or decrease according to the seasons.
During the spring, one should enter the fire-samādhi (*tejo-samādhi*) to warm the body.
The firelight is fierce and intense, and the body is steaming with heat; it is necessary to treat this.

Visualize that all the firelights become wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*) emerging from the pores, and between each flame there appear golden lotuses, upon which transformation Buddhas sit and preach the methods for treating illness.

With three kinds of jewels: first, the moon-essence maṇi; second, the starlight maṇi, which is like a celestial star, white in radiance and blue in body; and third, the crystal maṇi. One should visualize these three jewels: one illuminating the head, one illuminating the left shoulder, and one illuminating the right shoulder.

Having seen the three jewels, one visualizes that light from the three jewels issues from the pores of the body, becoming extremely cool and refreshing; with body and mind made supple, one enters the Fire Samādhi without being harmed by it—this is called the method for the Great Fire-Subduing Samādhi.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, during the autumn one should enter the earth-samādhi.
Upon entering the earth-samādhi, one perceives these signs of the earth:

The hundred-thousand-stone mountains, the iron mountains, the Cakravāḍa mountains, and the Vajra mountains—from head to foot—each of the three hundred and thirty-six joints constitutes a hundred-thousand mountains; at that time, one should swiftly treat the mountain deities and the precipitous cliffs.

Regarding the great method for cultivating the stages: one should contemplate each of these mountains individually and clearly, as if they were plantain trees; following this sequence, one should contemplate each one clearly according to the ten similes in the sutra.

At that time, the great earth of the ten directions appeared like white lapis lazuli, adorned with white jewel-flowers. Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, and Kātyāyana were seen sitting within a white vajra-cave; they walked upon the ground as if it were water, and for the practitioners, they expounded the five breakings and the five unions, and taught the impermanence of the earth.
When the practitioner has seen this, his body and mind become supple, and he regains his original mind; this is called the Great Dharma of Cultivating the Ground.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when the practitioner enters the Water Samādhi, he sees his own body like a great gushing spring, with its three hundred and thirty-six joints flowing away with the water. He sees the ground of the ten directions filled with blue, green, white, or red water; he ought to cultivate it with urgency."

As for the method of subduing water, one should first visualize the body as a maṇi jewel, a vessel of auspiciousness with golden flowers covering its top, causing the waters of the ten directions to flow into the vessel.

From this auspicious vase emerge seven flowers with seven distinct stalks; between each stalk are seven springs, within each spring are seven golden flowers, and upon each flower sits a Buddha preaching the seven factors of enlightenment. This is called the Great Dharma for Subduing Water.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a practitioner enters the wind-samādhi, he sees his own body become a nine-headed dragon; each dragon head has nine hundred ears and immeasurable mouths. From the pores of his body, his ears, and his mouths—resembling great ravines—fierce winds issue forth. He should urgently apply a remedy for this."
As for the method of treatment: one should instruct the practitioner to visualize his own body as a vajra-throne, and from its four sides, imagine four vajra-wheels to sustain this wind.

Furthermore, from the golden wheel, seven vajra-flowers arise; upon each flower, a transformation Buddha appears holding a ritual pitcher (*śikya*). Within each pitcher is a six-headed dragon that stirs its body to inhale the wind, causing the winds of the ten directions to become calm and motionless.

At that time, the practitioner again sees the seven Buddhas and the four great śrāvakas, who once more explain the seven factors of enlightenment and how to gradually enter the eightfold noble path; this is called the Great Dharma for treating internal wind. By contemplating the softness of the four elements as if they were filled with ghee, one gradually enters the noble stages and the realm of *jñeyāyatana*.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there is a practitioner whose four great elements become coarse and rough— whether through anger or joy, sorrow or laughter, or even by crawling on the belly or passing wind— one should instruct them to treat such ailments with urgency."

"As for the method of cultivation: first, one contemplates the thin skin, observing it starting from half a joint; its ninety-nine layers are like bubbles of air. Next, one contemplates the thick skin;
its ninety-nine layers are like the trunk of a plantain tree.
Next, one again contemplates the membranes; they are like cataracts over the eyes, their ninety-nine layers appearing as if about to burst through."

Next, one further contemplates the flesh, which likewise has ninety-nine layers, like the leaves of a plantain tree; within it are insects finer than an autumn hair, each with four heads, four mouths, and ninety-nine tails.

Next, one should contemplate the bones, seeing them as pure white as white lapis lazuli, with ninety-eight layers; four hundred and four vessels enter between the bones, flowing up and down like the fibers of a plantain tree.
Next, one should contemplate the marrow, which has ninety-eight layers, like the silk threads of an insect's web.
"Having observed the various joints, one next observes the skull: beneath each hair, four hundred and four channels enter directly into the brain;

the remaining thin skin, thick skin, and bone are no different from those of the body, except for the fourteen layers of the meninges and the brain itself, which is divided into four parts and consists of ninety-eight layers, with the four hundred and four channels flowing into the heart."

One should contemplate each of the large intestine, small intestine, spleen, kidneys, liver, lungs, heart, gallbladder, throat, the fatty tissue of the lungs, the two receptacles of the raw and the cooked, and the eighty thousand families of worms, making them all empty and void, bright and pure; with skin enveloping skin, the interior is as clear and radiant as white lapis lazuli.
"In this manner, one contemplates each bone joint individually until all three hundred and thirty-six joints are clearly understood, causing the mind to remain settled;
furthermore, one repeats this process one thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine times."

Thereafter, one should gather the vital energy (*prāṇa*) into a single point and regulate the breath through counting. One should visualize a Brahmā King holding a Brahma-flask, accompanied by a host of Brahmās, who comes before the practitioner and hands him a vajra-sword.

Having obtained the blade, he gouged out his own skull—which was as large as a horse's conch-shell—and placed it upon his left knee; from within a Brahma-vessel, white lotus flowers emerged, with nine nodes, nine stalks, and nine layers.

There was a youth who followed behind the Brahma King, emerging from the first lotus; his body was white like a person made of white jade, and he held a white pitcher in his hand, within which was clarified butter (*sarpis*).

“From within the wish-fulfilling jewel atop the Brahma-King’s topknot, medicinal herbs of various colors emerge and are placed into the clarified butter (sarpis). The youth pours this over [the patient], and it enters through the crown of the head, flows down into the cranial channels, and descends directly until it reaches the half-joint of the big toe of the left foot.”
When one joint is filled and thoroughly moistened, it extends even to the thin skin; then it reaches another joint.
In this manner, it gradually fills half the body;
once half the body is filled, it further fills the entire body.

Once the entire body is filled, the various medicines flow through the four hundred and four channels, and one contemplates that the three hundred and thirty-six joints of the body are all completely saturated.
At that time, the practitioner takes the skull back and places it upon the head; the youth then applies blue-colored medicine to the head, and these drops enter through the pores.

"Fearing that external winds might enter, Brahmā King further instructed him to prepare snow-mountain butter (*himavat-sarpis*), making it entirely bright white; its finest essence (*sarpis-manda*) flowed like crystal walls. He was to hold this to protect his body forty-nine times (seven times seven). Furthermore, he was to expand this into a great pool of clarified butter (*ghṛta-kuṇḍa*), with white butter serving as its flowers. The practitioner sat upon a canopy of butter within a cave of butter, while Brahmā King’s compassionate medicine was scattered throughout the intervals of the butter."
"Having thus contemplated this nine hundred and ninety-nine times, you should then further visualize the second joint.

Within the lotus is a red-colored youth who scatters red medicinal powder among the hair and throughout all the pores of the body, causing the red medicine to enter from the thin skin down to the marrow, making the area below the heart luminous and gradually softening the entire body."

"In the third section, a lotus blooms again; the golden youth takes yellow medicine and scatters it among his hair and throughout all the pores of his body, causing the yellow medicine to enter through the thin skin and reach even the marrow. It causes the area below the heart to turn blue, and it gradually increases throughout his entire body, becoming further and further supple."

"In the fourth section, the youth Vaiḍūrya holds blue-colored medicine in his right hand; he scatters it among his hair and throughout all the pores of his body, causing the blue medicine to enter through the thin skin and reach even the marrow, making the area below the heart red."
"Insert a single needle into each and every pore; insert two needles upward from beneath the feet.
Form three lotus flowers above the heart; within these three flowers are three fire-jewels emitting red light. This light shines upon the heart, causing it to gradually grow warm."

Thereafter, insert three needles into each joint of both palms, following the flow of the vessels up and down to harmonize the various qi, thereby generating the four hundred and four channels, while ensuring that the large intestine and kidney vessels are not disturbed and continue to flourish.
He further pierced the left intestinal vessel with five needles.

In this manner, the youth harmonized all the needles; through inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable cultivation, he drew them out and placed them beneath his five claws, then rubbed and touched the body of the Universal Wandering One (Viśvāmitra) with his hands.

"In the fifth section, a green youth holds a jade flask in his hand and pours green medicine through the anus, permeating the large and small intestines, the five viscera, and all the channels; this liquid then flows back out through the anus."
Various impure insects flow along with the water without damaging the *amṛta* (clarified butter);

when the insects stop and the water is exhausted, one further scatters green medicinal powder from between the hair and throughout all the pores of the body, causing the green medicinal powder to enter through the thin skin down to the marrow, making the area below the heart white and gradually increasing the softness throughout the entire body.

"In the sixth section, a purple-colored youth holds a rose-gem flask filled with rose-water, which he uses to thoroughly wash all the channels, causing the rose-water to emerge from every pore; all the insects beneath the skin emerge along with the water."

Furthermore, he takes a dry medicinal powder the color of amber and scatters it among his hair and throughout all the pores of his body, causing the amber-colored dry powder to enter through the thin skin and reach even the marrow; he causes the area below his heart to become as bright as the light of white snow, and his entire body gradually becomes increasingly supple.

"In the seventh section, a yellow youth grasps a vajra-drill and drills beneath both feet, drills both palms, and drills both sides of the heart. Thereafter, he takes the King of Cintāmaṇi jewels and rubs and polishes the six sense faculties; all the faculties open to receive the bliss of the supreme flavor of dhyāna. Between all the skin and veins, it is as if white ointment has been applied, and everything becomes supple."

"In the eighth section: The Youth of Vajra-Color holds two vases in his hands and pours the vajra-colored medicinal elixir into both ears and all the pores. Following the method of massage, he regulates the various joints; his body is like a chain as it moves through the intervals between the joints."

"In the ninth section, the youth Mani-colored emerges from the mouth of the flask and approaches the practitioner; he inserts his five fingers into the practitioner's mouth, and from the tips of those five fingers, five-colored medicinal elixirs flow forth."

After the practitioner has drunk, he contemplates his body and mind, as well as all the channels, as pure as a clear mirror, such that even the colors of crystal or *maṇi* jewels cannot serve as a simile.
The youth then gives the practitioner a lotus stalk to eat; when eating it, he follows the method for eating lotus roots, and from every drop flows the nectar of immortality.
Having consumed this stalk, only nine flowers remain; within each flower is a Brahmā King who brings a Brahmā throne and presents it to the practitioner, commanding the practitioner to sit upon it.

Once he has sat upon this seat, a great canopy of the seven treasures covers the practitioner from above, and each of the Brahma Kings expounds the Dharma-gate of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to instruct him.

By the power of the Brahma Kings, the Buddhas of the ten directions stand before the practitioner and preach loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, administering the medicine appropriate to his faculties to soften his four great elements.
He addressed Śāriputra:

“You should skillfully uphold this method of the soft four great elements for subduing the ninety-eight latent tendencies, which cures all illnesses within and without the body—the Brahmā-King Consecration and the Butter-Spilling Rite—and explain it to the fourfold assembly.”
At that time, Śāriputra, the Venerable Ānanda, and the others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Regarding the method for treating choking: "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

If an *āraṇyaka* bhikṣu applies his mind with excessive urgency, counts the breaths too coarsely, or sleeps insufficiently, and due to external wind and cold, or due to the movement of the spleen channels, the spleen, kidneys, and other vessels, various tendons give rise to wind; the qi becomes inverted and the chest is constricted; water flows through the joints and stagnates within the chest; and consequently, blood and qi become agitated, causing headaches, fullness in the back, and the contraction of all the tendons—he should treat this condition promptly.

"The method for treating this is as follows: first, one should take rich, oily, and delicious worldly medicines; then, lying on one's back, one should practice counting the breaths to achieve concentration. One should visualize Lake Anavatapta, its waters overflowing, filling an entire yojana, with a bed of golden sand and four kinds of jewels, and a golden wheel upon which golden lotuses bloom as large as chariot wheels."

Within the flowers are four precious beings—beasts with elephant trunks, lions, horses, and oxen—from whose mouths water flows. These flow around the pond seven times. Between the heads of these four beasts lies the seven-jeweled palace of the Naga King Anavatapta.

"From within the wish-fulfilling jewel atop the Dragon King’s head, by the power of the Dragon King, one thousand five hundred lotuses of various colors arise—five hundred of which are blue lotuses. Upon each, one of the five hundred arhats, such as the Venerable Piṇḍola, sits. At dusk they close, and during the day they open; there is a canopy of the seven precious gems above each bhikṣu, and a bed of the seven precious gems beneath each lotus."

There were five hundred golden lotus flowers, upon each of which sat one of the five hundred śrāmaṇeras, including Cunda and others; they closed at sunset and opened during the day, with canopies of the seven precious gems above the śrāmaṇeras and couches of the seven precious gems beneath the lotuses.

There were five hundred red lotuses; upon each sat great Arhats such as the Venerable Upānanda and Vasumitra, or, according to some accounts, five hundred members of the retinue of the Great Bodhisattvas. These flowers closed at dusk and opened during the day. Above the bhikṣus were canopies made of the seven precious gems, and beneath the lotuses were couches made of the seven precious gems. Furthermore, a high platform made of the seven precious gems, eight thousand *zhang* in length, emerged from below.

"In front of the palace of the Dragon King Anavatapta, there were five hundred youths upon its terrace, their bodies the color of pure gold. The first youth was named Jambha; the second youth was named Sudhana; and the fifth hundredth youth was named Abhiṣekabala."

“If the King wishes to treat the disease of choking, he should first bring to mind the one thousand five hundred elders, such as the Venerable Piṇḍola, as previously described, until they are clearly seen. Then, the Venerable Piṇḍola shall take this boy Jābāla to the Dragon King Anavatapta and fetch the white ambaṭha medicine; the ambaṭha medicine has a flavor like sugarcane, its shape resembles lotus roots, and its taste is also like rock honey.”
Having taken this medicine, his choking ailment was cured, the four elements were harmonized, and his eyes became clear and bright.

"If one gives rise to the mind of the Mahāyāna, the five hundred youths such as Jambū and Sudhana will preach the Mahāyāna Dharma for them; by means of this, they shall see the sixteen virtuous men such as Bhadrapāla, and also see the thousand bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, including Maitreya."
Because they had resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and were endowed with the six *pāramitās*;

whereas for those who had resolved their minds toward the state of a *śrāvaka*, the Venerable Piṇḍola taught them the Dharma of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and within ninety days they attained the stage of *arhat*.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“You must carefully receive and uphold this method for treating choking; be careful not to forget it.
At that time, Śāriputra, Ānanda, and the others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Dharma for treating the affliction of lust in practitioners; the Dharma for treating the affliction of lust in practitioners.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a practitioner enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), if thoughts of desire arise, the wind of lust moves through the four hundred and four channels (*nāḍī*). From the eyes to the body-faculties, they all shake simultaneously; the various sense-faculties become obstructed, stirring the winds of the mind and causing the mind to become deranged."
Because of this, one becomes insane and possessed by malevolent spirits; day and night, one’s thoughts of desire are as urgent as if one were trying to extinguish a fire on one's head.
One must treat this with haste. The method for treatment is to instruct this practitioner to contemplate the womb.
The womb (garbhāśaya) is located below the stomach and above the large intestine; it consists of ninety-nine layers of membranes, like the bladder of a dead pig.
Four hundred and four channels (nāḍī) issue from the womb, spreading out like the roots of a tree to all its branches.

It is like a bag filled with excrement, possessing one thousand nine hundred joints resembling the leaves of a plantain tree. Eighty thousand families of worms surround the four hundred and four channels as well as the womb itself.

It is like a horse's intestine reaching down to the birth canal; shaped like a bracelet on the arm, it is circular in size, rounded at the top and tapering to a point at the bottom, resembling the teeth of a shell.
It has ninety-nine layers, and within each layer dwell four hundred and four worms; each worm has twelve heads and twelve mouths.

When a person drinks water, the essence of the water enters the channels and is distributed among the various worms; it reaches the crown of the *vīra* worm and proceeds as far as the birth canal. Every half-month, impure water is expelled, which the worms each vomit up like putrid pus.
It enters the mouths of ninety worms and emerges from the six orifices of twelve worms, appearing like a flow of putrid crimson liquid.
Furthermore, there are various insects smaller than the finest autumn hair that sport within it.

Due to the evil karmic offenses of these men in their past lives, four hundred and four channels spread from the eye-organ to the four limbs, flowing through the various intestines down to the lower part of the raw-receptacle (āmāśaya) and up to the upper part of the cooked-receptacle (pakvāśaya).
"In the lungs and kidneys, on each side, there are sixty-four worms.

Each worm has twelve heads and twelve mouths; they are coiled and attached to one another, shaped like finger rings, filled with blue pus that resembles the semen of a wild boar—its foul stench is unbearable."

Reaching the region of the male organ, it divides into three branches; two branches are above, like the leaves of a plantain tree, possessing one thousand two hundred channels. Within each individual channel, wind-insects arise, as fine as the down of an autumn hair, resembling the beak of a *vilanda* bird.

"Within the mouths of various worms there arise sinew-colored worms; these worms have bodies resembling sinews that connect and sustain the womb, are able to move the various vessels, and absorb and discharge essence. There are seventy-eight thousand male worms, which are blue-white, and female worms, which are red-brown, coiled around one another like a stack of rings, resembling the *gośīrṣa* bird. They have ninety-eight eyes, and their vessels surge upward from the heart to the crown of the head."
"O men, when the eye contacts forms, the wind stirs the faculty of the mind; the four hundred and four channels are driven by the wind, moving and turning without ceasing."

Eighty thousand families of worms simultaneously open their mouths, and from their eyes, various pus flows through the veins down to the crowns of the worms' heads; the worms tremble and convulse, crazed and unconscious, as they touch the female organ—the male seed, which is blue and white, is the tears of these worms, and the female seed, which is yellow and red, is the pus of these worms.
"This is the dharma cultivated by the perfuming of the ninety-eight latent tendencies;
it is the eighty thousand families of worms, along with earth, water, fire, and wind, that perform these actions.
Thus he addressed Śāriputra.

“If there are members of the fourfold assembly who clothe themselves in the garment of shame and remorse, who take the medicine of shame and remorse, and who desire to seek liberation and transcend the suffering of the world, they should study this Dharma as if drinking ambrosia.”

"One who studies this dharma should visualize the aforementioned womb, up to the female organ and male body parts, with all the large and small worms opening their mouths, pricking up their ears, glaring with eyes wide open, and spitting out pus."
Turn it over with the hand and place it at the edge of the left knee; count the breaths to settle the mind and contemplate it one thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine times.

"Then, turning his hand over again, he used it to cover his head, causing these various worms and manifold impurities to first enter both eyes, ears, nose, and mouth, reaching every place without exception."

“Having seen this, one regards beautiful women and beautiful men, even up to sons of gods and daughters of gods, as if seeing a leper with *nālikā* sores and maggots, as having the appearance of the *ardhatālajaṅgha* demons with arrows from hell, or like the fierce, blazing fires of the Avīci Hell.”
"You should carefully observe your own body and the bodies of others; the impurity of the physical constituents of all sentient beings in the desire realm is exactly like this.
He addressed Śāriputra:
"Do you now understand?"
The fundamental seeds of the body-faculty of sentient beings are entirely impure; they cannot be fully described, but one should simply count the breaths and contemplate them with a single mind.

If one takes this medicine, one becomes a great man, a teacher of gods and humans, and a master who tames others; one escapes the mire of desire and is not swept away by the waters of the outflows or the great river of affectionate love, nor is one harmed by the calamitous, illusory forms of lewd and seductive demons.

"You should know that this person has not yet emerged from birth-and-death; yet their body is as fragrant and pure as the *utpala* flower. The Method for Treating the Wound of Gain and Honor.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there is a practitioner who is scorched by the fire of greed, and the poisonous arrow of gain and honor is blown and driven by an evil wind to pierce his heart."

Due to the causes and conditions of greed, the mind may become inverted; throughout the six periods of day and night, one contemplates the means for gratifying greed, like a cat watching a mouse with no sense of satiety, or like a seven-step snake whose body is covered in venom it has spat out.

For such an evil person, the subtle and smooth sensations of gain and offerings cause five hundred venomous snakes to gather within their body; from moment to moment, the poisonous fire of their mind blazes forth without ceasing.

Day and night, during the six periods, the fierce winds of affliction blow upon the fuel of gain and honor; within his heart they blaze without ceasing, while various serpents vie with one another to burn the sprouts of his roots of goodness.

Due to these causes and conditions, the madness and the fierce, burning venom of the black demon become intense; seeing others obtain gain is like an arrow piercing the heart, like a thorn entering the eye, or like a nail driven into the ear.

When the various sense-faculties are obstructed, five hundred and five snakes, four great venomous dragons, five bandits with drawn swords, and six village rākṣasas all compete to act simultaneously; because of this, one becomes insane and must be treated with urgency.

"The method for treating this is as follows: first, one should practice counting the breaths and bind the mind to achieve concentration. One should visualize an image one zhang and six chi in height—of purple-golden hue and possessing the thirty-two marks—sitting upon a precious lion throne within a cave of the seven treasures on Vulture Peak Mountain, preaching the Dharma for the removal of greed to the fourfold assembly."
He addressed them, saying:
"Sons of the Dharma!

Behold the kashaya robes, the six requisites, and the various implements worn by those who are greedy. They are like a forest of thorns and needle-seams; within them shall grow sword-trees, hundreds of thousands of iron nails, and iron-jawed insects that peck and devour their bodies."
Molten copper cauldrons, boiling brine, iron saws, and iron beds shall be your seats;

boiling excrement, venomous snakes, iron balls, cauldrons of molten liquid, forests of knives and halberds, billions of thorns, rivers of fire and flowing copper, and ash-slush with pus and blood shall be your food and drink.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these words, he remained silent and made no sound, causing the practitioner to see his own body lying within seven layers of iron cities. He saw five rākṣasas with their mouths agape facing both directions, using eighty iron tongs to pull out their tongues;
immeasurable iron plows, shaped like sword-trees, were plowing those tongues.

From between the armor of iron oxen, molten copper flowed forth; within the bodies of the iron executioners was pus of a hundred thousand colors, and the various worms within that pus were beyond counting.
Upon observing these things, his heart was struck with terror and his hair stood on end.

Whether emerging from or entering meditative concentration, he saw the robes he wore as being composed of pus, excrement, and blood; they were adorned with iron-beaked insects, forests of knives, and halberds.

He saw the food he consumed as being like worms; from his ears issued pus, excrement, urine, and various kinds of blood. There were eighty types of insects—wind-insects, fire-insects, water-insects, earth-insects, hell-insects—and all these insects vomited pus and poison that filled his *pātra* bowl.
Iron balls and swords and halberds serve as their fruits and melons.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Birth and death are not severed, Because of greed for and attachment to flavors.”
Nurturing an enemy leads to the grave, where one undergoes all manner of suffering in vain.
The body stinks like a corpse, with nine orifices flowing with impurities;
like a dung-worm that delights in filth, the fool’s craving for the body is no different.
The wise should contemplate the body, Without craving or defilement for the world;
Free from entanglements and free from desire— This is called true nirvana.
As all the Buddhas have taught, One should practice with single-minded devotion.
"Counting the breaths in a quiet place—this is called practicing the dhūtas.
He then told Śāriputra:

"The injury to the body and the destruction of a person's roots of goodness caused by gain and offerings cannot be fully described; one should simply count the breaths and contemplate with a single-minded focus."

If one takes this medicine, one becomes a great man, a teacher of gods and humans, and a master who tames others; one escapes the mud of desire, is not swept away by the waters of the fetters or the great river of affection, and is not burned or harmed by the ill omens of greed for profit.

It should be known that such a person has not yet emerged from birth and death; yet their body is as fragrant and pure as the *utpala* flower, surpassing the scent of human "fragrant elephants," dragon kings, *malla* wrestlers, and Maheśvara, and is revered by great powerful men, devas, and humans alike.

The Dharma for Treating the Transgression of Precepts:

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās receive the prohibitive precepts of the Buddha, yet their bodies and minds become deranged like a monkey—just as the method of planting has not yet reached growth when one plucks the branches and destroys the roots—the seven assemblies are likewise so.

Regarding the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts, before the 'color of the precepts' (śīla-rūpa) has even arisen, they commit duṣkṛta offenses up to pārājika; they are like a drunken elephant that avoids neither good nor evil, knows no directions, and tramples and destroys all things that are wholesome and excellent."

The fourfold assembly is likewise; they trample and destroy the pure precept-pool of blue lotuses. Their violation of the precepts is so fierce and rampant that they are like mad dogs, who, seeing people, trees, or even birds and beasts, pursue and bite them.

"When a person who has transgressed the precepts sees the Buddha, an Arhat, or a pure bhikṣu—a field of merit—and pursues them with insults, slanders, and vilification, they will drink their own poison, blood will appear all over their body, and fire will blaze up at every joint."

Mad, foolish, and lacking wisdom, they are moved by the fierce winds of the fetters that shake the mountain of afflictions—their eyes being greed and lust, their hands and feet hatred, and their bodies ignorance—as they trample upon the world, planting seeds of evil. Having planted them themselves, they further instruct others to seek them out as well.

The hell-wardens, rākṣasas, ox-headed ābhangas, the evil ghosts of the kalpa-ending fire, the deities of the sword-forest, King Yama, and the eighteen lords of the hells will constantly act as one’s great friends and supreme spiritual mentors (kalyāṇamitra), and one will certainly dwell day and night with such beings of the hells.

"This person of broken precepts, whose heart has already been entered by the fierce fires of all evils, for the sake of gain and fame, falsely claims to be virtuous and endowed with majestic power; he approaches those who dwell in *āraṇya* and know the Dharma, like a magician who deludes the eyes of others."

This deceitful person falsely practices *dhūta* austerities; the evil winds of broken precepts blow the flowers of sinful karma constantly upon him, while the fragrance of harsh speech and slander, and the incense of unwholesome thoughts, permeate his body and mind.

This person’s body and mind are like the *eranda* tree; resembling hundreds of thousands of insects or dogs, although they practice meditative concentration, they falsely manifest the objects perceived through counting the breaths.

At the very beginning, they see black Buddhas like the feet of a black elephant, or see people covered in ash; they see various bhikṣus with their heads split open and legs broken, and they see bhikṣuṇīs adorned with flower garlands.
He sees celestial elephants transformed into monkeys, with fire blazing at the tips of their fur, coming to touch and disturb him.
Or he sees a wild fox and a jackal, each with hundreds of thousands of tails, and on the tip of every tail are immeasurable insects of various kinds and foul appearance.
Or they may see emaciated camels, donkeys, pigs, dogs, kumbhāṇḍas, and other such beings;

or various evil yakṣas, rākṣasas, and executioners, each wielding various weapons and foul fires to strike and pummel the bhikṣu, whereby he becomes insane—sometimes singing, sometimes dancing, lying on the ground in filth, or committing various other evils—and one should treat this promptly.
"As for the method of treatment: the practitioner should go before the wise ones and sincerely confess the evil and unwholesome karma they have committed.
The wise ones should instruct this bhikṣu to bring to mind Śākyamuni Buddha, and so on, up to bringing to mind the seven successive Buddhas;
having brought the seven Buddhas to mind, he should then bring the thirty-five Buddhas to mind."
Thereafter, one should further bring to mind all the bodhisattvas and the mind of the Mahāyāna.
Contemplating the dharma of emptiness, one should feel deep shame and remorse, imagining each Buddha holding a water pitcher and pouring its contents over one’s crown.

Furthermore, one should imagine oneself falling into the Avīci Hell and undergoing various sufferings within the eighteen hells; while in those hells, one should invoke "Namo Buddha," "Namo Dharma," and "Namo Bhikṣusaṃgha," and practice the six recollections. Then, all Buddhas and Tathāgatas will emit white light from between their eyebrows within one's dreams to rescue one from the suffering of hell.

Having seen this, like a debtor who feels shame and ought to repay his debt, he should with single-minded devotion take off his saṃghāṭī robe, put on an antarvāsaka, and go before the pure monks. Prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground like a collapsing great mountain, he should, with a heart full of shame, repent for all his transgressions and perform various menial services for the Saṃgha—such as sweeping latrines and carrying away excrement—for a period of eight hundred days.
"Then, one should again bathe the body and put on the saṃghāṭī robe.

Entering the stūpa, with a single-minded focus and palms joined, one should contemplate the light of the Great Man’s mark of the white tuft between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows for one day up to seven days. Then, returning to the wise person, one should seek and request repentance."
The wise one should say: "O Bhikṣu!
You should now examine your own body as being like a golden jar containing four venomous snakes—two above and two below—spitting forth poison in a terrifying manner."

Again, he visualizes a six-headed dragon coiled around the vase; the dragon also spits venom that drips into the mouths of the snakes. Great trees emerge from the golden vase in the four directions, pervading the triple world.
"A black elephant comes again, wishing to uproot this tree, and fire breaks out on all four sides.
Having seen this occurrence, you should say:
"Bhikṣus, you should know:"
The golden vase is the vapor of the earth;
the blue snake arises from the wind element and is the poison of the wind element;
the green snake arises from the water element and is the poison of the water element.
The white snake arises from the earth element; it is the poison of the earth element.
The yellow snake arises from the fire element; it is the poison of the fire element.
The six-headed dragon is the five aggregates and space within your own body.
"This body is poisonous, harmful, and impure; why do you indulge in evil, violate the precepts, and fail to discipline yourself?

Having spoken these words, he further instructed him to sweep the stupa, smear the ground, and perform various menial labors, and additionally taught him to contemplate the Buddha, until he saw the Buddha emitting golden light and stroking his head with his hand.

Only then should one teach the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). Once the gateway of impurity has been thoroughly mastered and all obstacles are gone, one may then recite the precepts within the Saṃgha.
When wishing to recite the precepts, one should proclaim these words:

"The bhikṣu so-and-so and the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so have already performed arduous labor for eight hundred days and have contemplated the white tuft of hair between the Buddha’s eyebrows for seven days; they have perfected the contemplation of the poisonous snake and the perception of the hells."

Furthermore, he observed one Buddha preaching the method of repentance, the gate of impurity meditation, and the mirror of non-self and non-person; he again attained thorough penetration within these realms.
The Buddha poured water from his ritual pitcher onto the bhikṣu’s head, and a celestial deity appeared in a dream to declare that he was already purified.
"Now that I have felt shame and remorse, I have realized my error; I only pray that you will grant me your forgiveness.
At that time, the *vinayadhara* (master of discipline) should further examine this person according to the *vinaya*, and instruct him to recite the precepts.
"After reciting it eight hundred times, one will then be no different from the bhikṣu Ru-jing.
He addressed Śāriputra:

"If any member of the seven assemblies violates a minor precept and does not repent after two nights have passed, that person, though practicing dhyāna and samādhi in their present body, will ultimately not attain the Way."

If one violates a grave precept, one falls into the great hells; upon emerging from the hells, one receives the body of an animal. Having fully undergone such states for a complete three kalpas, one is then born as a human being.

Even though one has obtained a human body, for seventy-seven lifetimes one may be poor, afflicted with leprosy, unable to see the Buddha, unable to hear the Dharma, and lacking in the sense faculties.
Therefore, a wise person who violates a precept of the Buddha should feel dread toward even a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) as if being struck by a sword, and should harbor the utmost shame and remorse.
How much more so for the grave precepts?
If one can take this medicine of upholding the precepts, you should know that such a person is a man of supreme shame, modesty, and patience, whom none can surpass.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"With a broken precept and an impure mind, Like a thief-dog, they seek gain and offerings everywhere; Slain by their own greedy hearts."
One should take shame and remorse as medicine, wear patience as one's garment, adorn oneself with the flowers of repentance, and perfume oneself with the incense of a virtuous mind.
With single-mindedness, contemplate the marks of the Buddha; thus suffering is removed, and there will be no more sorrow or pain.
One should likewise contemplate the dharma of emptiness and cultivate the mind through the meditation on impurity.
This is called the nectar-consecration medicine of all Tathāgatas;
those who consume it will have no sorrow in their hearts and shall reach the shore of Nirvāṇa.
One should practice in accordance with the Dharma and not perform what is contrary to the Dharma;
whether in this life or in future lives, those who practice the Dharma attain liberation.
Following what the Buddha has taught, one should uphold the precepts and practice the dhūtas.
"With body and mind free from unwholesome conduct, one will swiftly attain liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"Receive well this medicine for treating violations of the precepts; be careful not to forget it."

*The Dharma for Regulating Music*.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."

If the fourfold assembly delights in various musical performances and never tires of such entertainment, this will cause the winds to stir—like a runaway horse, like a dog in autumn, or like the king of the *enīli* deer. Becoming addicted and deluded by folly, their minds become like sticky glue, following after objects everywhere and impossible to restrain; they must be treated with haste.

As for the method of cultivation: first, visualize a celestial maiden of peerless beauty, with various musical instruments naturally appearing in her two hands, producing ten thousand kinds of sounds.

Having seen this, the practitioner perceives that these celestial maidens surpass external forms by hundreds of millions of times, and hears their celestial voices which are peerless in the world; consequently, he becomes deluded and attached, contemplating their forms and listening to their sounds.

For this reason, one should be taught to contemplate the objects arising from the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) of this woman. By the power of counting the breaths (*ānāpāna*), one sees that the lovely eyes give rise to six venomous snakes which emerge from the eye-faculty and enter into the ear-faculty.
Furthermore, one sees two insects shaped like owls that let out a great, evil cry; they split open the head and take out the brain, scrambling to devour it.
Within the remaining four faculties, one sees cats, mice, dogs, and jackals scrambling to devour [the objects].

Because of this, one comes to see all female forms as foul, exposed, and impure—the thirty-six impurities—wherein the womb and its parasites serve as the woman’s ornaments; one sees the various musical instruments held by women as they lie rolling in excrement, and the wriggling of the worms within them sounding like the howls of jackals; their speech is so monstrous that it cannot be listened to, being like the wailing of rākṣasīs. Because of this, one develops weary detachment.
They should go to a wise person, confess the evil and unwholesome karma they have previously committed with a sincere heart, and repent.
The wise person should then instruct them in the contemplation of impermanence.
Thus he addressed Śāriputra:
"Receive well this method for treating music; be careful not to forget it.
At that time, Śāriputra, Ānanda, and the others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Dharma of Delighting in Verses and Praises: "Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a practitioner delights in composing verses and praising with beautiful tones—just as the wind moving the leaves of a *sāla* tree produces harmonious and elegant sounds, with a voice like that of Brahmā that gladdens the ears of others, using pleasing words that cause others to rejoice."

Driven by these winds of arrogance and conceit, their minds are like tangled weeds, wandering incessantly with the winds of the afflictions; they raise the banner of pride, beat the drum of self-importance, and toy with the fragments of the channels, thereby falling into madness—like a foolish monkey gathering flowers and fruits, their mind never resting for a moment and unable to count their breaths. You must treat this swiftly.

As for the method of treatment: first, one should visualize a tall banner made of the seven precious gems. At the top of this banner stands a gandharva, his body like white jade, moving his body to chant verses of praise. From the pores of his body emerge great lotus flowers, upon which hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus produce ten thousand kinds of sounds—a hundred-thousand-million-fold louder than one's own voice. By means of this, one gradually subdues their arrogance.
"The wise one should further instruct the practitioner to contemplate the tip of the banner with clarity, seeing a crystal mirror at its summit.
Those bhikṣus who rely on their voices, being arrogant and impure in mind, transform into rākṣasas who emit great, evil cries, with fire issuing from their mouths."

Furthermore, yakṣas came from the four directions, pulling out tongues and taking hearts to place upon the tips of banners; their hearts trembled violently as they wailed and cried out like the trumpeting of intoxicated elephants, or again with faint voices like the chanting of piśācas.

Because of this, they further hear various beautiful sounds, such as people crying out, calling for their parents, or uttering unprincipled abuse; because of this, they feel weary and detached, finding no pleasure in hearing them with their ears, and giving rise to thoughts of renunciation.
"The wise should instruct others to contemplate the eight sufferings as explained in the 'Contemplation of the Eight Sufferings.
He addressed Śāriputra:
"You should well receive this method for treating songs, chants, and verses of praise; be careful not to forget it."

[Regarding] the cause for the great and violent onset of dysentery being pacified, and the cause for the great and violent onset of dysentery being pacified: "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
If any member of the fourfold assembly enters the *apsamādhi* (water-samādhi), water emerges from their entire body such that neither body nor mind is visible, resembling the great ocean.

When emerging from this concentration, they find food and drink unpalatable, suffer from heat in the lower abdomen, experience increased agitation in the water-vessels (*āpō-dhātu*), and endure incessant diarrhea; these should be treated with prompt medical care.
"The method for treating this is to visualize a golden-winged bird; the bhikṣu mounts it and travels fearlessly across the great ocean, while all the nāgas and rākṣasas flee in terror."
The Garuḍa king ate the dragon; because the dragon was terrified, he sucked up all the water until it was gone and transformed himself into four snakes.
The Garuḍa king bit the four snakes in his beak, while the bhikṣu sat upon them, seeking water but finding none.

The king of the garuḍas emitted fire from his eyes to incinerate the snakes; the snakes were struck with terror—like illusory figures created by a magician vanishing and becoming invisible—and entered the body of the bhikṣu.

Upon emerging from this meditative absorption, one should take worldly medicines that purge the lower parts of the body. One should visualize two fire-jewels: one in the stomach channel to warm all the vessels, and one at the anus, shaped like a hot stone.
One should further visualize the Snow Mountain deity named Uḍaka, six zhang in height, white as jade or snow, holding a fragrant medicine called Sahānaga and bestowing it upon the practitioner.
When taking this medicine, first resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of bodhi.
Once the medicine has been taken, the four hundred and four diseases shall not move for the rest of one's life;
how much more so those that are minor?

"If you wish to cause that deity to arrive swiftly, you should bathe and purify yourself, refrain from eating the five pungent herbs, abstain from drinking alcohol, and avoid eating meat; then, in a quiet and secluded place, single-mindedly count the breaths, recite the name of that deity, and contemplate the image of that deity."

From one day to seven days, the Great Deity of the Snowy Mountains, together with twelve deities of white light and others, will come before the practitioner; they will first preach the Dharma for them, then bestow the medicine, and further instruct them in the twelve gates of dhyāna.
All those deities are great Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage.

"If there is one who is ill, they should first call to mind the deity Uttara-ga, and then successively call to mind the twelve White-Radiance deities: the deities Vīra, Balavat, Śūra, Jñānacārin, Vaśavartin, Subāhu, Kumāra, Durjaya, Śvetaprabha, Śvetaprabharāja, and Bhaiṣajyarāja."
Having seen them, he asks each of those deities about different Dharma-gates.

Those deities first cause the practitioner to see Maitreya Bodhisattva; at the place of Maitreya Bodhisattva, he sees Mañjuśrī and all other bodhisattvas, as well as the Buddhas of the ten directions.

"If this person did not commit the four grave prohibitions in past lives and does not violate the four grave prohibitions in the present life, they shall see the traces of the Path upon seeing the various deities."

If there are those who have violated the precepts, these divine kings will instruct them to perform repentance; after a full thousand days, they shall then be able to see Maitreya Bodhisattva and the great beings such as Mañjuśrī, and subsequently attain the fruits of the Path.
He addressed Śāriputra:

“If there are practitioners who, because of water, develop the four hundred and four ailments, and wish to cure them, they should quickly take this medicine, such as sāha and others. This will eliminate the illness without further affliction, extinguish the ocean of karmic obstructions, and allow for the swift realization of the traces of the Path.”
"Therefore, you should all receive and uphold this well; be careful not to forget or lose it.

The Method for Treating Headaches, Eye Pain, and Deafness Caused by the Fire Element. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."
If a practitioner enters the Fire Samādhi, flames arise from every joint; the large and small intestines simultaneously ignite, burning and agitating the fire-vessels (*agni-nāḍī*).

Upon emerging from this meditative state, the head experiences slight pain, the various vessels contract and twitch, the eyes turn red, and the ears become deaf. Because of these conditions, illness may arise; one should treat it promptly.

"As for the method of treatment: first, visualize a single lapis lazuli jar filled with water of various colors and blooming flowers of diverse precious gems. Upon each flower are hundreds of thousands of manifested Buddhas, and each of the manifested Bodhisattvas emits light from their white tufts of hair, illuminating all the flames of fire and causing those flames to transform into golden dragons."

Upon seeing this, the practitioner immediately felt great joy and formed a mental visualization of the jar—placed beneath the fire with the flower pedestal on top. He went before the Buddha and reached out his hand to grasp the jar; his hand became cool and refreshing, whereupon he cast his entire body toward the side of the jar to pay homage to the Buddha.

He then beheld the emanated Buddha emitting light from between his eyebrows, raining down drops of nectar that sprinkled upon all his joints; wherever the drops fell, they transformed into lapis lazuli. As the nectar flowed into the large intestine, both the large and small intestines became filled with it. The fiery glow gradually subsided, and various precious flowers sprang forth; these jeweled flowers were radiant, their colors being red and white.

"Furthermore, one should visualize Maheśvara riding a golden ox and holding a precious water-jar, approaching the practitioner. Within the water are various medicines called 'Poison-Destroyers,' which he causes the practitioner to ingest."

Furthermore, he held a jewel named Candra-maṇi (Sòng: Yueling, "Moon Essence") and placed it upon his crown; from it flowed various medicinal substances that were poured into his ears, eyes, and nose, so that by merely seeing him once, one was immediately cured.

Maheśvara—a great bodhisattva who constantly sports in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi—then emitted a great radiance from between his eyebrows, manifesting as a Buddha image. Five hundred rishis attended upon the World-Honored One, who, for the sake of practitioners, expounded the Dharma of the Gate of Ambrosia for treating illnesses.
