The Dharma for curing those who, upon entering the Samādhi of Entering the Grounds, see inauspicious signs and become so terrified that they lose their minds. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

If a practitioner enters the earth-samādhi, they see black mountains on the four sides; within the crevices of these mountains, there are immeasurable and boundless kumbhāṇḍas crouching upon earthen mounds, manifesting hideous forms with their various bodily organs and limbs clearly displayed.

Furthermore, there are five mountains that yakṣas vie with one another to seize; the kumbhāṇḍas, seized by intense pain and terror, let out a great, malevolent cry toward the place where the practitioner is.
Furthermore, one sees various ghosts with disheveled hair, clutching great iron clubs with mountains upon their tips, approaching the place where the practitioner is.
One also sees yakṣas carrying mountains on their shoulders and dancing.
The rākṣasa took the tree and went to where the yakṣa was; the rākṣasa, filled with rage, fought with the yakṣa.
The piśāca ghost wore a black mountain upon his head and held a dead tiger in his mouth.
When the practitioner sees this, his heart is struck with alarm and his hair stands on end.

Because of this terror, the rākṣasas become even more fierce; they battle with the yakṣas, and the rākṣasas emerge victorious. They sever the heads of the yakṣas and use the hands and feet of the piśācas as necklaces, and use the bodies and organs of the kumbhāṇḍas as flower garlands. They dance and leap before the ground; their canine teeth protrude upward like the branches of a sword-tree, hail falls from their eyes, and bolts of lightning burst into flame.

The yakṣas were even more formidable; they seized the rākṣasas, flayed their facial skin, gouged out their female organs, severed the male organs of the kumbhāṇḍas, and used the hands and feet of the piśācas to fashion flower garlands. They strung these around their ears and necks, danced before the ground, shook their bodies, and let out great shouts, emitting a most terrifying and evil sound.

Furthermore, he saw Vimalā, the mother born from the deities of the four great oceans, lying supine upon the ocean waters—possessing a thousand heads, each with two thousand hands and feet—stretching her body out toward the four directions, displaying her female organs; her formidable, jagged form was like a mountain smeared with blood.

Those various evil hairs were shaped like sword-trees, from which grew a tree like a forest of knives and mountains. From within it emerged hundreds of thousands of immeasurable *kumbhāṇḍas* with donkey ears, ox heads, lion mouths, horse feet, wolf tails, and *kumbhāṇḍa* bodies—such beings as these ghosts came forth from there.
Furthermore, he saw hundreds of thousands of great dragons, each tens of *yojanas* in length, emerging from within.

He also saw a ghost resembling a hundred beasts, its form like that of a lion, possessing ten thousand feet; amidst its scales were countless hundreds of thousands of venomous snakes, all emerging from within.
Again, he saw hungry ghosts, their forms ten billion yojanas in height and breadth, spitting poison and fire, emerging from within while carrying various mountains upon them.
He further saw a thousand wolves, joined at their tails yet distinct in body, with fangs as sharp as stone points, emerging from within.
Again, he saw a thousand tigers, each with a head at its tail; their entire bodies moved sideways as they emerged from within.
Again, he saw a dragon maiden, her body adorned with jeweled necklaces, most pleasing to the eye, emerging from within.
Yakṣas come forth from it to take food, as do wildcats, cats, mice, monkeys, jackals, foxes, malevolent spirits, evil ghosts, and all manner of predatory beasts.

The deities of the Avīci Hell and Mount Vajrāśmaka, the deities of the eighteen hells, nine billion ox-headed *ābhangas*, eight billion hungry ghosts, a thousand billion intestinal worms, and five hundred billion roundworms—such various manifestations as these, including loathsome spirits who wield mountains of blades, grasp sword-trees, or shake Mount Sumeru, the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), and the Gandhamādana Mountains.

"The practitioner sees his own body filling the great earth; all three hundred and thirty-six joints are like high mountains reaching up to the Formless Realm, with water flowing forth from their centers."
The four great poisonous snakes sport in the water, emitting fire from their mouths;
ten evil rākṣasas run amidst the flames, blowing wind from their ears and wind from their anus, which stirs up all the mountains;
all the ghosts and spirits come forth, glaring with wrath and dismembering [the body] joint by joint.
“The practitioner may become terrified because of this and suddenly develop a madness.
If one perceives such a thing, it must be treated immediately.

The method of treatment is as follows: first, visualize a sun disk together with the Sun Deity (Sūrya-devaputra) riding in a palace made of the four jewels, performing hundreds of thousands of musical performances. It shines upon the Black Mountain (Kāla-parvata), causing the Black Mountain to gradually grow bright.”
Having visualized one day, one should again visualize two days.
Having visualized two days, one should further observe one’s own body as three hundred and thirty-six joints of white bone, white as the Snowy Mountains, with the sun shining upon those mountains.
One should further visualize a palace of four jewels belonging to the Moon Deva atop one’s head, with hundreds of thousands of attendants holding moon-jewels and placing them upon that head.
When this visualization is accomplished, one visualizes another sun upon the third mountain, no different from the one above;
having seen this sun, one further visualizes another moon upon the Snowy Mountain of the cranial bone, just as before.
Having seen the moon, one should further imagine that upon the fourth mountain there is another sun illuminating this Black Mountain (*Kṛṣṇaparvata*).

Having seen the sun, one should imagine that the mountains of white bones consisting of the three hundred and thirty-six joints of one's own body all have peaks facing one another, with the four corners all confronting each other; between each of these peaks, there is a moonlight.

The Son of Heaven takes hold of the two beads with his hands and holds them apart; likewise, he should settle his mind between each of the joints and bone-angles. For the duration of ten inhalations and exhalations, he contemplates them with precision until they are clearly perceived, seeing that within each single bone there are the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*), bright, pure, and lovely like jewels made of the seven precious substances.

"Once this visualization is accomplished, one further visualizes a king of the golden-winged birds (garuḍa) wearing a maṇi jewel upon its head, seizing four snakes and six dragons; the snakes are terrified and the dragons flee."

The spirits and deities of the various mountains were simultaneously startled and agitated, appearing like a mass of blackness—all of which was the retribution for violating the precepts in previous lives; one should diligently repent and strictly purify one’s *śīla*.
Because of the purity of their *śīla*, the radiance of the sun and moon becomes even more brilliant;

however, if they harbor evil thoughts, speak evil words, or commit a *duṣkṛta* offense, then black earth will rain down upon the *maṇi* jewel, dust will obscure the sun and moon, and the stars will cease to move.

The Asura King manifests nine hundred and ninety-nine hands and a thousand heads all at once, eclipsing the sun, moon, and stars so that they do not appear; this is called "retrogression," for he has been plundered by the sword of an evil mind, the fire of harsh speech, and the thieves of broken precepts.
"If you wish to take this supreme nectar-like medicine, you must first maintain the precepts and purify all your deportment, repenting of karmic obstructions and evil, unwholesome offenses.

Furthermore, you should bind the mind and fix the attention, sitting upright in one place, counting the breaths and restraining the vital energy, observing the three hundred and thirty-six joints as before, causing each joint to face toward its neighbor."
The stars, moon, and other celestial bodies are as previously described.

Furthermore, the mind becomes increasingly clear and sharp; one sees between each joint of the body a moonlight like a garment and starlight like threads, sewn together so that they adhere to one another.
One sees four suns arise, whereby two-thirds of the waters of the four great oceans are diminished.
Seeing five suns appear, Mount Sumeru melts away and the great oceans dry up;
seeing six suns appear, one perceives that these various mountains gradually melt away;
seeing seven suns appear, the great earth blazes intensely.
The various *pretas* and *rākṣasas* fly up into the air and dwell there as far as the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), with a banner of fire following behind them;
they further reach the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the fire likewise follows them there.

When they wish to go to the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), their hands and feet shrivel and burn away, falling into a mass of fire. As they utter a terrifying roar that shakes the great earth, when they enter this *samādhi*, the great earth trembles slightly, like the turning of a chariot wheel.

"Quickly stabilize the mind and visualize the three hundred and thirty-six joints as being like mountains of vajra; their form is more beautiful than Mount Sumeru, and neither earth, water, fire, nor wind can shake them. One sees only four serpents holding mani-jewels amidst these skeletal mountains."

At that time, one should first visualize the shadow of the Buddha; seeing the adamantine boundary (vajrapāṇi), there is a maṇi mirror at the tip of the adamantine banner, within which the shadows of the seven Buddhas of the past appear.

Furthermore, one should carefully contemplate the white tufts between the eyebrows of Vipaśyin Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, Viśvabhū Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha, and Śākyamuni Buddha. One sees the white tufts between the eyebrows of these seven Buddhas as the color of crystal; the water is exceedingly cool and refreshing, washing all the joints. As the water from the white tufts washes the three hundred and thirty-six joints, they become brilliantly pure white. Their color is so clean, fresh, and wondrous—like a crystal mirror—that nothing can serve as a metaphor for it.
"Because of this, one further sees five vajra-wheels at the tops of the seven-jeweled banners; emerging from below, they revolve in mid-air and proclaim the meaning of the Four Noble Truths.

Although one sees and hears this, one single-mindedly contemplates the mountain of white bones of one's own body, whereupon one immediately sees Śākyamuni Buddha pouring water from a ritual pitcher upon the crown of one's head;
the same occurs for the other six Buddhas."
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed him, saying:
"O son of the Dharma!
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering, empty, impermanent, and non-self; you should contemplate them with earnest attention."

Furthermore, he extensively expounded upon emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and desirelessness; he taught that the body is empty and quiescent, that the four great elements have no master, and that the five aggregates have no home, being ultimately extinguished and identical to space.
By this means, he immediately realized that impermanence destroys the world and contemplated the Four Noble Truths;
within five breath-cycles, he shattered twenty billion burning fetters and became a *srotāpanna*;
within ten breath-cycles, he was freed from the flow of all desires and became a *sakṛdāgāmin*.

Within the duration of ten inhalations and exhalations, one severs all dull fetters (*dauṣṭhulya*), the fetters of the desire and form realms, and the roots of all bonds (*saṃyojana*); not returning to the desire realm, one becomes a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Within those ten breaths, one sports in the dharma of emptiness with a mind free from attachment and obstruction, abiding in the thirty-four mental states associated with liberation; the ten fundamental roots are realized as neither extinguished nor destroyed, and the mountain of ninety-eight fetters is crushed.

The Great Valiant General, the Banner of Dharma of Wisdom-Light, arrived from the four directions; a vajra-jewel throne emerged from below, and as they touched one another, they expounded the Dharma of Emptiness.
Five vajra-wheels rested at the side of his left knee, spontaneously expounding the nine unimpeded knowledges and the eight liberations.
All the śrāvakas of the past entered the Vaiḍūrya samādhi and stood before him.
Śākyamuni Buddha extensively proclaimed the meaning and flavor of the meditative state that is like a diamond;
thereupon, becoming tranquil, he became invisible in body and mind and entered the Diamond Samādhi.

Arising from the vajra-samādhi, the mountains of fetters collapse, the roots of affliction are severed, the river of ignorance dries up, and the slave of old age and death is extinguished. Birth is forever ended, the holy life is established; like refined gold that no longer accepts various desires, one has accomplished what was to be done—this is called a Great Arhat.

"If one gives rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta, at first one will see the light from the ūrṇā-kośa of the seven Buddhas; the white-light radiance of each Tathāgata divides into ten branches, manifesting ten jeweled flowers, jeweled trees, and jeweled terraces that stand in rows in the sky."

At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions likewise emitted light and water, washing the joints as described above. From within the white-hair rays (*ūrṇā-kośa*) of each Buddha, they proclaimed eighteen kinds of Dharma-gates of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), eighteen kinds of Dharma-gates of great compassion (*mahā-karuṇā*), eighteen kinds of Dharma-gates of great joy (*mahā-muditā*), and eighteen kinds of Dharma-gates of great equanimity (*mahā-upekṣā*).
Once they have gradually grown and been instructed, he teaches them to cultivate the four immeasurable minds;
having perfected the four immeasurables, he explains to them the ten kinds of luminous minds;
once they have perfected the luminous minds, he instructs them that form is itself emptiness, and that emptiness does not arise from the extinction of form.
Having contemplated emptiness, one teaches the six dharmas to bodhisattvas;
having practiced these six dharmas, one cultivates the six recollections, recollecting the Buddha’s Dharma-body;
having recollected the Buddha’s Dharma-body, one gives rise to the mind of dedication.
Once the dedication is accomplished, one establishes the four great vows not to abandon sentient beings;
once the four vows are accomplished, one fulfills the bodhisattva precepts;
once the bodhisattva precepts are accomplished, one studies and cultivates the semblance dāna-pāramitā.
Once the dānapāramitā has been perfected, one studies and cultivates the ten pāramitās that resemble them.

When this visualization is accomplished, one contemplates internal emptiness and external emptiness; therein, one presently beholds hundreds of thousands of immeasurable Buddhas pouring water over one’s head and binding turbans upon one’s head, as they preach the Dharma of emptiness.

"By means of the mind of emptiness, one awakens and enters the stage of a bodhisattva; this is called the 'Stage of Nature' (dharmatā-bhūmi)—the initial realm of a bodhisattva. Many give rise to overweening pride (*abhimāna*) regarding this dharma; you should recognize that this is the characteristic sign of the initial realm of the bodhicitta. He addressed Śāriputra:

"This is called the Samādhi of Cultivating the Ground (*bhūmi-parikarman*), which extinguishes the overweening pride and the terrifying characteristics of the three poisons—the mother of ignorance. You should receive and uphold it well; be careful not to forget or lose it."
At that time, Śāriputra, Ānanda, and the others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
[The Great Dharma for Treating Wind Disorders. Furthermore, Śāriputra: "The Great Dharma for Treating Wind Disorders: Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
If a practitioner enters the wind-samādhi, they see within their own nine orifices winds of five colors emerging like great ravines and valleys.

They further see their own three hundred and thirty-six joints as white as the Snow Mountains; from each joint, winds emerge as various *ai-ji-chi*. *Ai-ji-chi* refers to the *utthāna-piśāca*, the "corpse-raising ghost."
The various Aikishis, grasping iron clubs in their hands and wearing necklaces of a thousand skulls, arrived at the practitioner's location together with ninety-eight kinds of nāgas and ghosts.
When the practitioner sees this, his heart will be startled and his hair stand on end; he may consequently become insane or afflicted with leprosy, and must treat it promptly.
As for the method of treatment: one should first contemplate the four great sages of the Snowy Mountains and the Fragrant Mountain, all of whom are indeed great bodhisattvas.

Visualize that seer’s body as golden-yellow in color and sixteen *zhang* in height; his right hand holds a flower and his left hand holds a vajra-wheel, while his mouth contains fragrant medicine, shielding the practitioner so that the wind does not arise.

The rishi took flowers and recited mantras over water, which he brought forth; the dragon then sucked up all the winds until its body swelled so large that it lay prostrate on the ground, unable to rise.
One should contemplate this dragon as being like a plantain tree, with layer upon layer of skin enveloping one another, such that it cannot breathe.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this mantra:

*Namo buddhāya | namo dharmāya | namaḥ saṃghāya | namo mahāriṣivijarāja | aiduta dadata | samanta vajarakeśi | dhara guṭa śiṭa | carī carī | mahācarī umare umaleke | siddhambe yambe | ayambe liyuk yukke | sarvadhāraṇike | āśrute makule ye ye mumu mumu mumu muha ha.* When the World-Honored One had finished speaking this mantra, he addressed Śāriputra:

"This divine mantra has been spoken by immeasurable Buddhas of the past; I, too, now speak this mantra in the present; and in the future, the Bodhisattvas of Maitreya’s Worthy Eon shall likewise proclaim it."

The merit of this divine mantra is like that of Maheśvara; it can cause the evil bhikṣus of the five hundred years of the later age to attain a pure mind and intention, harmonizing and properly regulating the increase and decrease of the four great elements. It also cures the four hundred and four diseases within the mind, the objective realms arising from the four hundred and four channels, and the seeds of desire and temperament of the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Furthermore, it cures karmic obstructions and all evils of violating the precepts, so that they are forever exhausted without remainder.

This is called "The Dhāraṇī for Thoroughly Healing the Seventy-two Kinds of Illnesses and Afflictions"; it is also called "The Dhāraṇī for Uprooting the Root of Ignorance of the Five Aggregates"; and it is also called "The Dhāraṇī for Directly Beholding All Buddhas and Śrāvakas Preaching the True Dharma to Destroy All Fetters."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The nature of phenomena has no basis; Contemplating emptiness is likewise so.
If one can contemplate the four great elements In this way, one will not be slain by the latent tendencies.”
Taking medicine and practicing meditative concentration,
reciting this dhāraṇī and single-mindedly mindful of all Buddhas, the fetters shall never again arise.
The ocean of afflictions shall be forever exhausted, and the river of craving and attachment shall also be cut off.
All desires have no cause; they claim for themselves liberation.
With a mind free from affliction and tranquil, they sport in the six supernormal powers and, by means of dhāraṇīs, instruct others.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: "You should now know this:

after my parinirvāṇa, if there should be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās in future ages who hear this profound and secret essential Dharma of pure śīla, as well as the methods and medicines for curing the various ailments of practicing dhyāna-samādhi—namely, this *Glorious King Victorious Banner Dhāraṇī*—you should know that such persons have not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas alone. Rather, they have long cultivated the three kinds of bodhicitta in the presence of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and it is now that they hear this profound and secret essential."
It should be known that for one who practices as taught, this is their final body; like a swift-flowing stream, they will quickly attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya and the conduct of a bodhisattva.
When the Buddha spoke these words, five hundred Śākyaputrakas further advanced and attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

Among the one thousand śūdras in the city of Śrāvastī who had gone mad due to their past practice of dhyāna, they immediately conceived joy upon hearing what the Buddha said and attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.

Eight billion devas were cured of the four great ailments; their bodies and minds were free from affliction, and they immediately gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*). They rained down celestial flowers from all sides, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly.
At that time, the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings in the assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, spoke these words with one voice:

"The Tathāgata has appeared in the world precisely to subdue these rākṣasa-like practitioners of mad, evil, and heterodox views, so that they may regain their original minds, becoming as lovely and delightful as fine flower-banners."
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
Like the udumbara flower, you appear but once in an age.
At that time, the great assembly praised him with these verses:
"The Crown Prince of the Solar Clan, scion of the Ikṣvāku lineage, nephew of the Moon from Starlight, and son of Queen Māyā.
At birth he took seven steps; his feet treading upon the earth, they shook the great trichiliocosm."
The deities of the ten directions responded, and thirty-two auspicious omens appeared.
He abandoned his kingdom as if it were spittle and sat beneath the Pippala tree at the supreme Vajra site of enlightenment, subduing trillions of māras.
Having attained the path to enlightenment, with a face as pure as the full moon and the stains of the mind forever exhausted,
I now pay homage with a single-minded heart to the most excellent among the Śākyas, who is endowed with supreme compassion.
"It can cause all sentient beings to forever escape the suffering of birth and death.

At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the fourfold assembly, the World-Honored One again earnestly extended his golden hand to stroke the heads of Śāriputra and Ānanda, entrusting them with this matter.
At that time, Śāriputra, Ānanda, and the rest of the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
[The Method for Treating Those Who Have Just Begun to Sit in Meditation and Are Possessed by Demons, Experiencing Various Disturbances and Unable to Attain Concentration] Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, at the lecture hall built by Queen Mallikā, a place inhabited by the Nālīlu demons.

When the thousand sons of elders, including Rāṣṭrapāla and others, first went forth into homelessness, they requested the Venerable Ānanda, Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, and others to serve as their preceptors. Mahākāśyapa then instructed the thousand bhikṣus to practice breath-counting in a quiet place.

Possessed by a malevolent spirit, he saw a ghost with a face like a lute, four eyes, and two mouths, its face emitting light; it struck and poked his armpits and other parts of his body with its hands, chanting aloud:
"Bu-ti bu-ti! (Bhūti bhūti!)
"Like a whirling firebrand or a flash of lightning, it arises and ceases, causing the practitioner's mind to find no stability.
If one perceives this, one must immediately treat it."

As for the method of treatment, one instructs this practitioner: when the *pūtana* arrives, they should close their eyes with single-minded focus and, remaining hidden, revile it, speaking these words:
"I now recognize you; I know that you are a fire-eater, a scent-sniffer, and a *steyalakṣmī* from within this Jambudvīpa."
"You hold wrong views and delight in breaking the precepts.
I now uphold the precepts; I shall never fear you.
If one is a renunciant, they should recite the Preface to the Precepts.
"If they are householders, they should recite the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, or the Eight Precepts; then the ghosts will retreat and crawl away.
At that time, having heard these words, Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One!"

Now, because this son of a householder, the bhikṣu, was taught by the World-Honored One the method for subduing the Bhūta-demon to escape all evils and not be bound or possessed by malevolent spirits,

future bhikṣus— after more than a thousand years have passed since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa— will wish to instruct bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās in the practice of counting the breaths in a quiet place, maintaining mindfulness of ānāpāna.

If various ghosts and spirits, for the purpose of disrupting the Path, manifest in the form of mice—either black or red—they claw at the practitioner’s heart, scratch their feet, hands, and ears, reaching every part of the body;
or they utter the cries of birds, or the moans of ghosts, or engage in secret whispering;
or there may be fox-demons who take the form of a newlywed bride, adorning their bodies to massage and adjust the practitioner’s limbs while preaching what is not the Dharma.
Sometimes they manifest as dogs, wailing and crying out without restraint;
sometimes they become eagles, vultures,
or hundreds of species of birds, making all manner of sounds— whispering, shouting, and so forth, their voices being diverse.
Or they may appear as small children, proceeding in groups of hundreds or thousands, or in tens, fives, twos, threes, or even singly; they produce various sounds and approach the practitioner.

Or one may see gadflies, flies, insects, fleas, snakes, or vipers; or they enter the ears like the humming of a queen bee, or enter the eyes like scattering grains of curdled milk, or else they touch the heart and create various forms of mental disturbance.
"Because of this, he has become deranged, abandoned his secluded dwelling, and engaged in heedless conduct;
how should he be treated? The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it for you."
“If there are members of the fourfold assembly afflicted by this ghost, you should explain to them the method for subduing ghosts.

This Pūtana ghost has sixty-three names; it was once a bhikṣu during the time of the past Buddha Kanakamuni who, while on the verge of attaining the stage of Srotāpanna, was expelled from the Saṃgha due to wrong livelihood. Dying in a state of anger, he vowed to become a ghost, and thus continues to harass the fourfold assembly until today.”
His lifespan shall be one kalpa; when the kalpa ends, his life will terminate and he shall fall into the Avīci Hell.
You all should today recognize his name, bind your mindfulness to him with single-mindedness, and do not allow yourselves to be distracted.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke as follows:
"Būṭi-būṭi is an evil yakṣa, also known as the Dream-Demon (svapnabhūta).
When one dreams of this and immediately loses semen, one should arouse a sense of repentance: [and recite the following]..."
“Futai comes! Because of past evil causes and conditions, I have encountered this transgressor and harmful ghost; I now lash my heart and bind my senses so that they do not become dissolute.”
"Such spirits, when dwelling in the void, are called 'void-dwelling spirits' (ākāśa-gandharva); when among beds and bedding, they are called 'belly-crawling spirits' (udaracara-gandharva).
Furthermore, they have three other names:
first, Gambhīra-kṣudraka-vakunaku-ni-le-ve-ghoṣa-ve-ghoṣa."
Molaka-sahava, the spirits of the quarters and paths, the chi-mei spirits, the wang-liang spirits,
the spirits that consume pus, the spirits that eat saliva, the water deities, the fire deities,
the mountain deities, the grove and garden deities, female spirits, male spirits, boy spirits, and girl spirits.
Kṣatriya ghosts, Brāhmaṇa ghosts, Vaiśya ghosts, Śūdra ghosts,
walking ghosts, inverted-walking ghosts, mounted ghosts, donkey-eared ghosts, tiger-headed ghosts,
cat-like-voiced ghosts, pigeon-dove ghosts, osprey-voiced ghosts, cormorant ghosts, and horned owl ghosts.
Or again, they may transform themselves into the eight classes of spirits and ghosts: the *vighna* (obstructing) ghosts, the *khara* (wasting) ghosts,
the eight-cornered ghosts, the white-mouse ghosts, the lotus-colored ghosts, the fox-demon ghosts, the spirit-possessing ghosts, the hundred-insect essence-demons,
the four evil *piśāca* ghosts, and the *kumbhāṇḍa* ghosts.
These sixty-three kinds of hideous spirits and ghosts are the names of these deities.

When ghosts cause disorder, one should practice counting the breaths to make the mind extremely tranquil; one should with a sincere heart mindfulness the seven Buddhas of the past and recite their names—namo Vipaśyin Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, Viśvabhū Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha, and Śākyamuni Buddha. Having recited the names of those Buddhas, one should then remember and uphold the Sarvarutakauśalya-dhāraṇī (the Dharani of All Sounds).
He then spoke the mantra:

“Ami ami karīṣa kṣāntir abhyuṣṭe huṃ svāhā | huṃ svāhā | mahākāruṇika-maitrāya bodhisattvāya. “If there are those whose minds are distracted and who are deluded by *bhūta* spirits—whether they manifest various illusory realms—they should recite and uphold this dhāraṇī, the names of the seven Buddhas, and Maitreya Bodhisattva. With single-minded attention, they should count their breaths and recite the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* one hundred times. These evil spirits will each be subdued, and they shall never again harass the fourfold assembly practicing the Path.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“You should well uphold this method for purifying body, speech, and mind, for subduing one’s deportment, and for expelling evil spirits. To ensure that the fourfold assembly of disciples may increase in virtue—so that they do not give rise to distracted thoughts and may enter into samādhi—you must receive and uphold it well; be careful not to forget or lose it.”
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. "Furthermore, Ānanda!

If, when a practitioner is sitting, he suffers from his two ears feeling full, pain in his joints, itching in the palms of his hands, pain in the soles of his feet, agitation in his lower chest and neck, or twisting of his tendons and dizziness of the eyes; or if *piśāca* spirits come to his seat to whisper in secret, or scatter incense and flowers to create various kinds of demonic apparitions—he should quickly treat these conditions."
"As for the method of treatment: first, one should visualize the two Bodhisattvas, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, holding golden vases and pouring water over [the practitioner].

Next, one should further visualize the Śvetaśaila King holding a single white flower and approaching the practitioner, covering their crown with it; as white light flows in and moistens the pores of the body, one immediately attains suppleness, and no other signs appear."

Thereafter, he again saw the youth Śava holding *ṛṣi-puṣpa* flowers and scattering them over the practitioner; from between each flower, various wonderful medicines rained down, moistening his pores. All ailments of the viscera, itching, various pains, faint voices, and all classes of ghosts and spirits were forever extinguished without remainder.

"Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata Bodhisattva expound for them the Mahāyāna Dharma of equality; the various mountain deities of Fragrant Mountain and Snowy Mountains, as well as the Jambuka youths, likewise teach them according to their faculties the various twelve-gate dhyānas, medicinal decoctions suited to their ailments, medical prescriptions, and incantations."

By means of this, one is able to see the Venerable Piṇḍola and the various Arhats, as well as the five hundred śrāmaṇeras such as Cunda and Upa, all arriving simultaneously at the practitioner's location; each of these Śrāvakas then expounds various methods for treating illnesses.
"Or perhaps there is an Arhat who, following the Buddha's instructions, teaches this bhikṣu to hollow out his crown of the head gradually until his entire body is empty, and then to fill it with oil;
a Brahmā holds a medicine—its color golden—and pours it over his body until he is full;
and the Bodhisattva, the King of Physicians, preaches various Dharmas."
If one gives rise to the mind of a śrāvaka, one will attain the stage of srotāpanna according to what Piṇḍola has said;
if one gives rise to the Mahāyāna mind, one will immediately attain the samādhi of the presence of all Buddhas according to what the two bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata have said.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if the fourfold assembly of disciples wishes to practice seated meditation, they should first sit upright in stillness for seven days, and thereafter cultivate the mind by counting the breaths for seven days."

Furthermore, one should take these medicines that eliminate illness and so forth: to eliminate sound and remove the diaphragm, to stabilize the mind and guard the intent, to cultivate the mind and cultivate the body, and to harmonize the primary elements so they do not lose their proper timing.

With single-minded devotion, one does not violate even minor precepts or rules of decorum; one guards the precepts one has undertaken as one protects one's own eyes, or as a gravely ill person follows the instructions of a skilled physician.

The practitioner is likewise; following the count, they increase it repeatedly without allowing for any regression or loss, as if their head were on fire. Complying with the words of the noble ones, this is called treating the illness by taking warm medicine for the body.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Receive and uphold this well; be careful not to forget or lose it.
When the Venerable Ānanda heard what the Buddha had said, he rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The younger cousin of the King of Hexi, the Upāsaka, the Great An-yang Marquis of the Juqu clan, while at the Vajra Āraṇya dwelling of the Kūmude Mahāvihāra in the kingdom of Yutian, met the Indian Bhikṣu, Mahāyāna Śramaṇa Buddhasena. This man was exceptionally gifted by nature, peerless within his own country, and could recite fifty million verses from memory. He was also profoundly learned in the methods of dhyāna; his knowledge encompassed both the internal and external teachings, such that there were no scriptures he had not mastered.
Therefore, the people of the world all said of him: "A lion among men!"
Juqu personally received the instruction and memorized it without impediment.
On the eighth day of the ninth month of the second year of the Xiaojian era, he transcribed this sutra at Zhuyuan Monastery, completing it on the twenty-fifth day of that same month.
